note: Real measured output from this development machine (16-core/24-thread i9-12900K, Windows). Evaluates WorkerPool's three execution backends: sequential (existing default), threaded (existing, use_threads=True), and process (new, Phase 5, use_processes=True). Commands: python benchmarks/benchmark_phase5.py --mode distributed --workers <N> --executor <sequential|threaded|process> --drones <N> --ticks 10 --warmup 3

threaded_vs_sequential.conclusion: Threading gives NO real benefit -- roughly matches or is slightly worse than sequential at every worker count tested. Python's GIL is not released long enough by these NumPy calls (many small per-partition arrays, not a few huge ones) to outweigh thread-scheduling/synchronization overhead.

process_vs_sequential.conclusion: A real ProcessPoolExecutor (bypasses the GIL entirely) measured a genuine speedup at 4-8 workers and 20k-100k drones -- 1.2x-1.9x depending on scale/worker count -- but is WORSE than sequential at 1 worker (pure process-pool creation/IPC overhead with no parallel work to gain from). This is why it is implemented as an explicit, off-by-default opt-in (DistributedConfig(use_processes=True)), not a replacement for the sequential default.
process_vs_sequential.best_case: 100,000 drones, 8 workers, process executor: 106.004ms/tick vs. sequential's best case (1 worker, 162.676ms/tick) = 1.53x faster than the fastest sequential configuration; 1.82x faster than sequential at the same worker count.

correctness: test_process_executor_multi_partition_matches_single_partition and test_run_movement_batch_process_matches_sequential / test_run_detection_batch_process_matches_sequential (tests/test_coordinator.py, tests/test_worker.py) assert byte-identical results between sequential and process execution -- the speedup is free, not a correctness trade-off.
decision: Implemented as an opt-in third executor (DistributedConfig.use_processes, WorkerPool(use_processes=True)), off by default. Not made the default because: (1) it regresses at 1 worker / small drone counts, (2) it requires the caller to call coordinator.shutdown() to avoid leaking processes, (3) Windows spawn semantics require the caller's entry point to be __main__-guarded. See README.md's Phase 5 section for full writeup.
